decision: Who the first version is built for
options: Weekly regulars who buy the same loaves
Anyone who wants to pre-order bread
Customers who've been disappointed by sell-outs
recommendation: Weekly regulars who buy the same loaves
reason: A third of artisan bakery visitors buy bread weekly, giving us a real base to build for rather than guessing at occasional buyers or sell-out patterns we haven't measured.
question: What makes someone a regular at this bakery rather than just a weekly bread buyer?

source.how_verified: Found with one Linkup search on 14 Nov 2026; the page was opened through Linkup's fetch (the build session's proxy refuses bakerybusiness.com directly) and the quote above is copied exactly from it.

text: Noor: found a source on a third of artisan-bakery visitors buy bread there every week.

decision: Whether to show bread that's sold out or low in stock
options: Show all breads with live stock levels
Show only what's available to order
Show everything, mark popular items
recommendation: Show only what's available to order
reason: We'd need to learn first whether seeing sell-outs motivates pre-orders or just frustrates people who came to buy now.

decision: Whether customers create accounts or order as guests
options: Account required for all orders
Guest checkout only
Account optional, guest allowed
recommendation: Account required for all orders
reason: Regulars ordering their usual every week need the system to remember them, and we can't deliver on that promise without accounts.

decision: How far ahead customers can place orders
options: Next day only
Up to a week ahead
Up to two weeks ahead
recommendation: Up to a week ahead
reason: Weekly regulars need to book their usual loaf for their usual day, and a week gives the bakery a clear baking plan without over-committing stock.

note: Worked out what we know about regulars at artisan bakeries, and what we'd need to learn first about pre-orders and sell-outs.

decision: What we track when a regular completes their order
options: Log order completion with items and timestamp
Log order completion with items, timestamp, and customer ID to spot repeat orders
Log order completion with full history: items, timing patterns, favourite breads, order frequency
recommendation: Log order completion with items, timestamp, and customer ID to spot repeat orders
reason: We need to know if regulars are successfully reserving their usual bread, which requires connecting orders to people over time.
question: How will we know if regulars are getting their usual loaves week after week?

decision: What single number tells us the browse step worked
options: Count unique visitors who view the bread list
Count visitors who select at least one bread
Measure time spent viewing bread options
recommendation: Count visitors who select at least one bread
reason: Browsing only works if it leads to picking something; views alone don't tell us the step succeeded.

decision: What we measure when someone picks their pickup time
options: Track time slot selections
Track time slot selections and whether customer changed their choice
Track time slot selections with preferred times by customer to learn patterns
recommendation: Track time slot selections
reason: We only need to know the step completed; pattern analysis isn't required to measure if this step works.

decision: Whether we verify actual pickups happened
options: Don't track pickups after order confirmation
Log when orders are marked as collected
Log pickups with timing data to measure late arrivals
recommendation: Log when orders are marked as collected
reason: We need to know if orders placed actually get picked up to measure end-to-end success and spot no-shows.

note: Measuring what matters from browse to pickup: track completed orders, know regular patterns, verify pickups

decision: Whether the site serves only established regulars or also welcomes new customers
options: Regulars only (login required, invitation-based)
Open to anyone who finds the site
Regulars prioritized but others can browse
recommendation: Regulars prioritized but others can browse
reason: Solves the core problem for regulars while letting the bakery grow its customer base without turning away interest.
question: What makes someone a regular worth designing for first?

decision: Whether customers choose specific pickup times or just pickup day
options: Specific time slots (9am, 10am, 11am)
Just the day (ready anytime that day)
Morning or afternoon windows
recommendation: Morning or afternoon windows
reason: Balances bakery workflow planning with customer flexibility and keeps the ordering flow simple.

decision: What happens when a regular's usual loaf sells out before they order
options: Show out of stock, no substitute
Suggest similar breads automatically
Hold stock for known regulars
recommendation: Suggest similar breads automatically
reason: Maintains the promise that regulars won't leave empty-handed while keeping operations realistic for a small bakery.
question: How does it feel when the bakery knows what you like but doesn't have it today?

decision: Whether the site remembers previous orders to speed up repeat ordering
options: Remember nothing, fresh each time
Show order history, one-click reorder
Pre-fill cart with usual items
recommendation: Show order history, one-click reorder
reason: Delivers on the 'they know your usual' promise without presuming what someone wants today.

note: Drafted product decisions from the journey flow: who it serves, what each step asks for, in/out scope, edge cases, and customer-facing words

decision: How order quantity limits are enforced when stock runs low
options: First-come gets full quantity, later orders rejected
All pending orders scaled down proportionally
Accept all orders, baker decides fulfillment
recommendation: First-come gets full quantity, later orders rejected
reason: Simple to build, clear to customers, matches the real-world scarcity they already know from the shop.
question: What promise are we making to regulars about getting their usual loaf?

decision: What happens when two customers claim the last sourdough simultaneously
options: First database write wins, second gets rejection
Both succeed, baker gets notification to resolve
Lock inventory during checkout flow
recommendation: First database write wins, second gets rejection
reason: Pessimistic locking adds complexity; optimistic concurrency with clear failure is boring and correct.

decision: Whether customers can modify or cancel orders after confirmation
options: No changes allowed once confirmed
Changes allowed until cutoff time
Changes allowed anytime, baker notified
recommendation: Changes allowed until cutoff time
reason: Matches bakery workflow (baking happens at a known time) without creating operational chaos.
question: How far ahead does the baker need to know final numbers to plan the bake?

decision: How customer identity is established across visits
options: Phone number only, no password
Email and password account
Device fingerprint with optional phone
recommendation: Phone number only, no password
reason: Simplest path for regulars who want their usual; phone is already needed for pickup coordination.

note: Template switches and backend logic for a live pre-order page where bakery regulars can reserve their usual bread.

decision: When customers pay for their pre-order
options: Pay in full when ordering online
Pay when picking up at the bakery
Pay a deposit online, rest at pickup
recommendation: Pay when picking up at the bakery
reason: Regulars already have a trust relationship with the bakery, and paying on pickup keeps the familiar pattern of how they buy bread now.
question: What does paying ahead feel like to someone who's been coming to the same bakery every morning for years?

decision: How bread is priced in the system
options: Same as in-shop prices
Pre-order discount to encourage adoption
Premium for guaranteed availability
recommendation: Same as in-shop prices
reason: This is about holding their usual loaf, not changing what they pay; a premium would break trust and a discount isn't needed when the value is guaranteed availability.
question: What makes this worth it for regulars if the price stays the same?

decision: Whether orders require a deposit to hold the bread
options: No deposit, order is a commitment
Small deposit per loaf, rest at pickup
Full payment upfront
recommendation: No deposit, order is a commitment
reason: For regulars the bakery knows by name, their word is enough; adding a deposit adds friction where trust already exists.
question: How does the bakery know who will actually show up for their bread?

decision: What happens if a customer doesn't pick up their order
options: No refund, bread is baked for them
Credit toward next order
Full refund, no penalty
recommendation: No refund, bread is baked for them
reason: The bakery bakes specifically for their order; no-shows cost the bakery real waste, and regulars understand this commitment.

note: Payment timing, pricing structure, and deposit rules for the pre-order system

decision: What the experience feels like: remembered regular vs first-time guided
options: Remembered: one-tap reorder of your usual, minimal explanation
Guided: step-by-step selection with descriptions and help
Hybrid: defaults for regulars, guidance when needed
recommendation: Remembered: one-tap reorder of your usual, minimal explanation
reason: The positioning is about regulars never facing sold-out loaves and the brand feel is 'like the baker already knows you', which means recognition over explanation.
question: What makes a regular customer feel recognized when they walk into the bakery?

decision: What leads each screen: product imagery vs minimal task focus
options: Large bread photos as hero images on each screen
Text-focused with small thumbnails only where needed
Product images only on browsing, clean forms elsewhere
recommendation: Text-focused with small thumbnails only where needed
reason: Sketch first polish last means deciding structure before styling, and taste-skill rules say carry headlines by size and tight tracking, not decoration.

decision: Empty state for first-time visitors with no usual order yet
options: Show full browse catalog immediately
Explain the regular concept then show browse
Simple 'Start your first order' with minimal copy
recommendation: Simple 'Start your first order' with minimal copy
reason: No filler words or mood paragraphs; buttons are verb and object; the interface stays 90-95% neutral with contrast from hierarchy not colour bars.

decision: Density of the bread list: compact scanning vs spacious cards
options: Compact list with small type for quick scanning
Spacious cards 24px apart with room for descriptions
Single column with 48px heading-to-content gaps
recommendation: Spacious cards 24px apart with room for descriptions
reason: Taste-skill spacing rules set cards 24px apart, and one card recipe keeps the interface consistent without creating three box depths.

note: Sketched the pre-order flow for regulars who want to guarantee their usual loaf.
